r5-m01.abandon: The mechanism says T 1.0 + min-p 0.1 brings loops back 'because it sharpens the head, not because it deletes tail tokens'. The board's own comparison holds the head fixed and changes only the tail. result-44b4df pairs every truncated cell with the same-seed untruncated cell at the same temperature ('paired vs same-seed min-p 0'). At T 1.0 the untruncated cell and the min-p 0.1 cell have the same pre-truncation distribution, so the same top-1 probabilities. The only thing min-p changes there is deleting tail tokens, and renormalising, which follows from the deletion. Yet result-44b4df reports: 'Truncating the tail at T 1.0 brings loops back (rule-A loops 0 -> 34 at min-p 0.1, 12 at top-p 0.95; cap hits 27 -> 58)'. Top-p 0.95 also deletes only the tail, and it too brings loops back (12). The head-only lock rule ('a loop locks only when the top-1 token keeps a probability above about 0.9 for a run of positions') is also contradicted by the untruncated T 1.0 cells, which have exactly that head and do not loop. result-5e17a6: 'Rule-A loops: 0 of 500 in either cell.' knowledge-787e53: 'At T 1.0 rule A finds 0 loops in T1, T2 and T3 (500 each)'. So a head above 0.9 is not enough to lock a loop when the tail is kept, and deleting the tail at a fixed head is enough to bring loops back. That is the opposite of the claimed cause. The external finding the mechanism would need agrees with the tail reading. 2610.24715: 'Pure sampling never locks', and the lock is created by the truncation threshold (escape probability exactly 0 once the loop token's probability reaches the threshold). The T 1.5 + min-p 0.1 result (0 loops) does not save the mechanism. Under min-p, a flatter head lowers p_max and so the cutoff p_base x p_max, which keeps more of the tail. That is a truncation-width account, not a head-only one. A theory built on 'not because it deletes tail tokens' would be tested against a contrast the board has already decided.

r5-m12.abandon: The mechanism needs the RL model to write line-start 'Answer:' markers before it verifies. Wang's rule reads a line-start 'Answer:' first and falls back to the LAST box. A model that only boxes is therefore read at its final marker, and earlier provisional boxes cannot cost it anything. The board shows the RL model does not write 'Answer:' lines; the base does. knowledge-499152: "'Answer:' line share base 0.44, RL 0.00" and "the base ends with an 'Answer:' line in 39-46 % of answers and RL boxes". knowledge-8229be: every arm that recovers RL accuracy takes RL's format, "'Answer:' line in 0-4 % of answers vs 39-46 % for base-like arms" (knowledge-69adda says the same). result-fdc8da: at the answer start RL gives the 'Answer:' form a log-prob gap of "'Answer:' line median -8.36 (n=132, 121 right)", against \boxed "0.000 (n=338)", so RL actively avoids that marker. result-c57b51: a gold-equal value sits in the last 5 lines of "31 of 2,000 base samples", "against 5 for RL", so RL rarely loses a right value while stating its answer. A first-marker rule can only hit the model that writes 'Answer:' lines, and that model is the base. result-60d899 already shows the literal rule costing the base: "a literal reading of their rule ... 336-355" against v3 405-418. So the direction the mechanism needs (the rule costs RL more than the base) is reversed on the measured pair. The one escape is that Wang's 3.0 release formats answers differently from 3.1. No item supports that. knowledge-8a31ad (7) says 3.1 differs from 3.0 only "by completion length 16k instead of 12k and by not masking truncated sequences", with the same reward and prompt. result-9d979a finds Math 3.0 and 3.1 are each other's nearest neighbours in weight subspace ("Math 3.0 with Math 3.1 0.476"). Using this mechanism to explain the Wang parity would require a 3.0 'Answer:' habit that nothing on the board shows and every format measurement argues against.
